proposals.evidence_note: Own retrospective Portuguese interview identifies actual reading and intellectual effect,alongside Vidal-Naquet,Vernant,Finley and travel. This second retrospective prompt is consolidated in the same influence pair; it establishes no exclusive origin or original Certeau text collation.

proposals.relationship: Hartog identifies Braudel’s writings on history as a resource for his own historiography teaching and reflection.
proposals.evidence_note: Own interview355 names La Méditerranée and especially Écrits sur l’histoire,which he read while teaching at Strasbourg after1975. He explicitly never attended Braudel’s seminar and had not originally worked in modern history;the interviewer’s implied early Indonesian Braudel influence is rejected. Original1949/1969works unread.

proposals.relationship: Hartog argues that Braudel’s hierarchy of historical durations and treatment of events should themselves be understood in their wartime and postwar setting.
proposals.evidence_note: Own interview355 historicizes the program while praising its enlargement of historians’ questions and denying that he means to denounce Braudel or reduce longue durée to refusal of war. This is a qualified challenge to treating the1950s–1960sframework as self-evident;not a claim that wartime context wholly explains it.

proposals.relationship: Hartog uses Koselleck’s tension between experience and expectation to formulate the problem of presentism.
proposals.evidence_note: Own interview363 explicitly reuses the categories while asking whether their relation has broken down and distinguishing provisional from fuller presentism. The formulation remains a question/heuristic,not a demonstrated universal sequence. Note29 cites a2006edition without a matching complete bibliography entry;original edition/work not guessed and unread.

proposals.relationship: Hartog uses Arendt’s image of a gap in time to explore whether presentism represents a pause or a more durable regime.
proposals.evidence_note: Own interview363 explicitly borrows the image while retaining uncertainty about its application. Editorial note28 points to a1961reference and Portuguese rendering,but supplies no complete matching bibliographic entry;no original edition or whole Arendt theory is invented. Original text unread.

proposals.relationship: Hartog uses Ricœur’s inquiries into narrative,time and historical representation as a resource for reflecting on historians’ own practice.

proposals.relationship: Hartog uses Ginzburg’s reflections on narrative’s cognitive powers and the interaction of evidence and storytelling in comparing historical approaches to representation.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2011article read in2013Portuguese translation16–18 explicitly credits a realism that is not positivism and reconstructs Ginzburg’s narrative practice. It coexists with a later objection about Aristotle’s Rhetoric;not whole-program agreement or formative mentoring. Cited French2003Rapports de force and2010Le fil et les traces remain unread.

proposals.relationship: Hartog questions whether Ginzburg’s linkage of rhetoric and proof establishes Aristotle’s Rhetoric as the primary ancient account of historiography.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2011/2013article20–21 examines Thucydides’ reconstruction of the remote past and Aristotle’s placement of inquiries within political deliberation. Hartog grants the importance of proof and Ginzburg’s narrative sophistication;his objection is a particular ancient-text interpretation,not equating realism with positivism. Original Ginzburg works and Greek-text editions not freshly read beyond Hartog’s translated quotations.
primary_locators: Aristóteles2013,20–21,from Detenhamo-nos through argument that inquiries concern politics rather than rhetoric.

proposals.relationship: Hartog argues that Ricœur’s extension of Aristotelian emplotment to historical narrative crosses the Poetics’ original separation of history from poetry.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2011/2013article21–22 calls this extension Ricœur’s philosophical right and recognizes his effort to preserve history’s referential intention through representance. It is a bounded interpretive disagreement,not accusation of fabrication or denial of Ricœur’s wider value. The negative effect of later historians’ deference is explicitly not assigned to Ricœur himself.
primary_locators: Aristóteles2013,21–22,paragraph beginning Para Ricœur and continuation;Interview2012,360,final qualification.

proposals.relationship: Hartog argues that White’s incorporation of historical poetics into rhetoric moves beyond Aristotle’s exclusion of history from poetic mimesis.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2011/2013article18–19 identifies the interpretive move while carefully distinguishing Ricœur’s and Ginzburg’s different readings of White. This is Hartog’s limited ancient/modern conceptual qualification,not wholesale rejection of narrative analysis or attribution of every anti-White argument to him. Metahistory and White’s complete corpus unread.

proposals.relationship: Hartog uses Foucault’s analysis of classical classification to develop his criticism of Veyne’s invariant method.
